title: USCIS Just Clarified That Most H-1B Holders Won't Have to Leave the US to Apply for a Green Card. The Relief Comes With a Catch.
excerpt: The agency outlined three conditions for staying — economic benefit, national interest, and individual circumstances — but none of them are precisely defined
body:
The United States Citizenship and Immigration Services has walked back one of the most alarming immigration policy signals of the year, clarifying on May 26 that most H-1B visa holders will not be forced to leave the country while applying for a green card.

The clarification came from USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler, who said that applicants who can demonstrate their work provides an "economic benefit or otherwise serves the national interest" would likely be allowed to continue their residency without interruption. "People who present applications that provide an economic benefit or otherwise are in the national interest will likely be able to continue on their current path," Kahler said.

## What Changed

The reversal addresses weeks of mounting anxiety among foreign workers — particularly Indian professionals who constitute the single largest demographic of H-1B visa holders in the United States. An earlier policy memo had implied that all temporary visa holders seeking permanent residency would need to return to their home countries to apply, a requirement that would have upended hundreds of thousands of lives overnight.

Under the original guidance, even professionals with decades of continuous residence in the U.S., mortgages, children in American schools, and spouses with their own careers would have been required to leave and apply from abroad — a process that can take months or years due to consular appointment backlogs.

## Three Conditions for Staying

USCIS outlined three primary conditions that could exempt applicants from the leave-and-apply requirement:

**Economic Benefit** — Applicants whose roles contribute positively to the U.S. economy can remain in the country during processing.

**National Interest** — Positions deemed to serve broader national interests qualify for continued residency.

**Individualized Circumstances** — Other applicants may still be evaluated on a case-by-case basis, though the specific criteria remain undisclosed.

## The Catch

Immigration attorneys are cautioning that the clarification, while welcome, introduces its own uncertainty. The terms "economic benefit" and "national interest" are not precisely defined, leaving room for inconsistent application across USCIS field offices. An engineer at Google in Mountain View and an engineer at a mid-size consulting firm in Ohio might receive different outcomes under the same policy.

The adjustment of status pathway has been the primary mechanism through which Indian professionals maintain their residency while navigating the notoriously long green card backlog. Indian nationals in the employment-based EB-2 and EB-3 categories routinely face wait times exceeding a decade due to per-country caps.

## The Diaspora Dimension

The policy reversal comes amid a charged moment for Indian Americans. Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu recently urged Indians in America to "choose self-respect" and return home, comments that drew sharp responses from professionals who pointed out the impracticality of abandoning established careers, homes, and their children's education on short notice.

For the estimated 300,000 to 400,000 Indian nationals currently in the H-1B-to-green-card pipeline, the USCIS clarification provides partial relief but not certainty. The policy landscape remains fluid, and immigration advocates are urging affected workers to document their economic contributions and maintain updated legal counsel.

The message from Washington is slightly less hostile than it was a week ago. Whether that holds through the next policy memo is the question nobody in the queue can yet answer.
author: Diaspora Desk
